1.pericope_label: And Abraham journeyed from thence toward the south country, and dwelled between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar — and Abraham said of Sarah his wife, She is my sister: and Abimelech king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah

schools.summary: Say he returned from the plains of Mamre, where he had lived fifteen or twenty years, into the more southern parts of Canaan, and that the reason of the remove is not certain. Some think he could not bear the stench of the sulphurous lake the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah had become; others that he was moved by the scandal of Lot’s incest with his daughters, which prejudiced the idolatrous people of those parts against the true religion; neither of which is likely, by reason of the distance. The better reason seems to be that it was so ordered in providence that he should remove from place to place, so that it might appear he was but a sojourner in the land. Or say the account of the destruction of Sodom was a digression, and that the history now returns to show what happened to Abraham and how the Lord protected him until the promised seed should be born; that he did not travel beyond the limits of the inheritance given him but went southward into the region which afterwards fell chiefly to the lot of Judah; and that though it is unknown what his intention was in removing, we ought to be persuaded he had not transferred his abode for any insufficient cause, especially since a son he had not even dared to wish for had lately been promised him. Allow the sulphur as a possibility, since the whole neighbourhood might well have been tainted, that men might the more clearly perceive this memorable judgment of God, so that Abraham, seeing the place under the curse, was drawn elsewhere by his detestation of it; and allow also that he may have been driven away by the malice and injuries of those among whom he dwelt, as happened to him in another place. On the lie, say he gave this out in all conversation he came into, and to every one who asked who she was, which was little better than a lie; it was at least an equivocation and a deception, not at all justifiable, and it tended to expose his wife’s chastity and discovered a distrust of divine providence — the same infirmity he had given way to in Egypt, and therefore the more inexcusable now, for good men not only fall into sin but have their relapses. Or set it out at greater length as a remarkable instance both of the infirmity of man and of the grace of God: it is a common proverb that even fools become wise by suffering evil, but Abraham, forgetful of the great danger which had befallen him in Egypt, once more strikes his foot against the same stone, although the Lord had purposely chastised him that the warning might be useful throughout his whole life. We perceive in the holy patriarch how easily the oblivion both of the chastisements and the favours of God steals over us, and it is impossible to excuse his gross negligence in not calling to mind that he had once tempted God, and that he would have had himself alone to blame if his wife had become another man’s. Yet if we thoroughly examine ourselves, scarcely any one will be found who will not acknowledge that he has often offended in the same way. Add the charge of ingratitude, since had he reflected that his wife was wonderfully preserved to him by the Lord he would never again knowingly have cast himself into similar danger, making the former favour, so far as in him lay, of none effect. But notice the nature of the sin: Abraham did not, for the sake of providing for his own safety, prostitute his wife, as impious men cavil; rather, as he had before been anxious to preserve his life till he should receive the seed divinely promised him, so now, seeing his wife with child and hoping to enjoy so great a blessing, he thought nothing of her danger.

Note the removal from Mamre, where he had lived nearly twenty years, into the country of the Philistines. We are not told upon what occasion he removed — whether terrified by the destruction of Sodom, or because the country round was for the present prejudiced by it, or, as some of the Jewish writers say, because he was grieved at Lot’s incest with his daughters and the reproach which the Canaanites cast upon him and his religion for his kinsman’s sake — but doubtless there was some good cause. Draw the lesson: in a world where we are strangers and pilgrims we cannot expect to be always in the same place, and wherever we are we must look upon ourselves but as sojourners. Then note his sin in denying his wife, as before, which was not only in itself such an equivocation as bordered upon a lie, and which if admitted as lawful would be the ruin of human converse and an inlet to all falsehood, but was also an exposing of the chastity and honour of his wife, of which he ought to have been the protector. And observe that it had here a twofold aggravation. First, he had been guilty of this same sin before, had been reproved for it, and had been convinced of the folly of the suggestion which induced him to it, and yet he returns to it — from which note that it is possible for a good man not only to fall into sin but to relapse into the same sin, through the surprise and strength of temptation and the infirmity of the flesh; let backsliders therefore repent, but not despair. Second, Sarah, as it should seem, was now with child of the promised seed, or at least in expectation of being so quickly, according to the word of God, and he ought therefore the more to have guarded her.

Say he journeyed from Mamre, where he had so long halted and which seems to have continued one of his homes; and since he had been commanded to traverse the whole land, we need seek no reasons for his removal, it being the rule of his life to move from place to place, both on account of his cattle and because by so doing he was taking possession of the country — though certain places were his head-quarters, such as Bethel, Mamre and Beer-sheba. Note that the south country is a proper name, the Negeb, and refer the reader to the earlier notes for Kadesh, Shur and Gerar. On the deception, observe that twenty years before he had acted in the same way in Egypt and had been rebuked, yet sent away with large presents; and note that a later verse of this chapter shows the false representation which twice brought them into trouble was habitual with the two, nor does Abraham ever seem conscious that he was acting wrongfully in it. To us it seems cowardly, in one who had so many men trained to battle, thus to expose his wife to danger, and to have recourse to deceit at the very time when such abundant revelations were being made to him also shows an apparent want of faith in God. But Holy Scripture neither represents its heroes as perfect, nor does it raise them disproportionately above the level of their own times; its distinguishing feature is rather that it ever insists upon a perpetual progress upwards, and urges men onward to be better and holier than those that went before. Abraham was not on the same high spiritual level as a Christian ought to be who has the perfect example of Christ for his pattern and the gift of the Holy Ghost for his aid, and the fact that God rescued him and Sarah from all danger in Egypt may have seemed to him a warrant that in future difficulties he would have the same divine protection. Human conduct is ever strangely chequered, but we have a wholesome lesson in the fact that it was Abraham’s politic device which twice entangled him in actual danger. On Sarah, note she was now ninety years of age and that naturally her beauty must have faded; some, however, think that with the promise of a son her youth had been renewed, while others suppose the purpose uppermost in Abimelech’s mind was political. Or run the narrative straight: Abimelech had not come near her, because God had hindered him by illness, and excused himself on the ground that he had done no wrong, since he had supposed Sarah to be Abraham’s sister on the word of both husband and wife — a plea admitted by God, who told him that He had kept him from sinning, and commanded him to restore the woman immediately to her husband, who was a prophet, that he might pray for him and save his life, threatening him with certain death to himself and all belonging to him if he refused.

Give the chapter its argument first: Abraham leaves Mamre, sojourns at Kadesh and Shur, and settles in Gerar; Abimelech takes Sarah, Abraham having acknowledged her only as his sister; Abimelech is warned by God in a dream to restore her, asserts his innocence, and is further warned; he expostulates with Abraham, who vindicates his conduct; Abimelech restores Sarah, makes Abraham a present of sheep, oxen and slaves, offers him a residence anywhere in the land, and reproves Sarah; and at Abraham’s intercession the curse of barrenness is removed. Then say it is very likely this holy man was so deeply affected with the melancholy prospect of the ruined cities, and with not knowing what had become of his nephew Lot and his family, that he could no longer bear to dwell within sight of the place; so, having struck his tents and sojourned a short time at Kadesh and Shur, he fixed his habitation in Gerar, a city of Arabia Petraea, under a king of the Philistines called Abimelech, that is my father king, who appears to have been not only the father of his people but a righteous man. On Sarah, say she was now about ninety and probably with child of Isaac, so that her beauty must have been considerably impaired since she was taken in a similar manner by Pharaoh; but that she was probably chosen now more on account of forming an alliance with Abraham, who was very rich, than on account of any personal accomplishments — for a petty king would naturally be glad to ally himself with such a powerful chief, whose late defeat of the four confederate kings was enough to establish his credit and cause his friendship to be courted; and what more effectual means could be used than taking the woman he understood to be Abraham’s sister to be his second wife, which in those times had no kind of disgrace attached to it? Elsewhere say only that we are not told upon what occasion he removed, and that the king of Gerar sent and took her to his house.

debates: Why Abraham left Mamre.
Whether the deception was an emergency measure or a standing arrangement.
What Abimelech wanted with a woman of ninety.
Whether Abraham can be excused for exposing his wife.
Whether a reason for the removal need be sought at all.
outliers: Ellicott dismisses the question of motive, since Abraham was commanded to traverse the land and moved as a rule of life.
Ellicott notes from a later verse that the false representation was habitual, and that Abraham never seems conscious of wrongdoing in it.
Ellicott argues that Scripture does not raise its heroes above the level of their own times, but insists on a perpetual progress upwards.
Calvin refuses the charge that Abraham prostituted his wife, and locates the sin in a preoccupation with the promised seed.
Clarke and Ellicott both suppose the motive political, an alliance with a chief who had lately beaten four kings.
Ellicott reports the alternative view that Sarah’s youth had been renewed with the promise of a son.
Gill weighs and rejects both traditional explanations of the removal on the ground of distance.

3.pericope_label: But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and said to him, Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man’s wife — but Abimelech had not come near her: and he said, Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation? — said he not unto me, She is my sister? and she, even she herself said, He is my brother: in the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands have I done this

schools.summary: Meet the critical argument first. From the use of this title of the Deity it has been said that this narrative is an Elohistic form of the Jehovistic narrative in the twelfth chapter; but even in the history of the Fall, where the writer so remarkably styles the Deity Jehovah-Elohim, he nevertheless restricts Eve and the serpent in their conversation to the name Elohim. With the same care in the application of the names, it is necessarily Elohim who appears to a heathen king, and had the title Jehovah been used it would have been a violation of the narrator’s rule. Moreover the sole reason for calling that narrative Jehovistic is that there it is Jehovah who plagues Pharaoh for Sarah’s sake; but equally here, at the last verse of this chapter, it is Jehovah who protects Sarah from Abimelech, in both cases the covenant God saving his people from injury. Then render thou art but a dead man as the Hebrew has it, thou diest, or art dying, and observe that Abimelech was already suffering from the malady spoken of at the end of the chapter when Elohim appeared and warned him that death would follow perseverance in retaining Sarah — it was this malady which caused the abstention. On the righteous nation, note the allusion to the fate of Sodom: though the malady was confined to Abimelech and his household, he sees destruction threatening his whole people, who compared with the inhabitants of the cities of the plain were righteous; and note the indirect proof of the truth of his assertion in the fact that death is acquiesced in as the fitting punishment for adultery. On the integrity of heart, observe that not only does Abimelech assert it but Elohim admits the plea — and yet this Philistine king indulges in polygamy and claims the right of taking the female relatives of anyone passing through his territory to add them to his harem. The words therefore mean no more than that he was not consciously violating any of his own rules of morality, and thus illustrate the gospel principle that men will be punished not by an absolute decree but equitably, according to their knowledge. Abimelech was doing wrong and was suffering punishment, but the punishment was remedial, for his advancement in right knowing and right doing. It is by means of revelation that men have attained a proper understanding of the moral law: though often called the law of nature, nature does not give it but only acknowledges it when given, and the inner light is but a faint and inconstant glimmering. Or else run the text straight, giving the verses and then the substance: Abimelech, who had not come near her because God had hindered him by illness, excused himself on the ground that he had done no wrong, having supposed Sarah to be Abraham’s sister on the word of both husband and wife; the plea was admitted, God telling him that He had kept him from sinning and commanding him to restore the woman at once to her husband, who was a prophet, that he might pray for him and save his life, with the threat of certain death to himself and all belonging to him if he refused. Abimelech carried out the divine instructions: the next morning he collected his servants and related what had occurred, at which the men were greatly alarmed.

Say God put a dream into his mind, by which he cautioned him against taking Sarah to wife, so careful was the Lord that no wrong should be done to so godly and virtuous a person, exposed as she was through the weakness of her husband; and correct the Jewish commentator who interprets this of an angel, when it was God himself. Note that she had been put into an apartment in the palace and not yet admitted to his company, and that another version reads had not touched her. Then draw the comfort: the Lord acted with such gentleness that in punishing his servant he yet, as a father, forgave him, just as he deals with us, so that while chastising us with his rod his mercy far exceeds his severity. Infer that he takes greater care of the pious than carnal sense can understand, since he watches over them while they sleep; and note carefully that however we may be despised by the world we are yet precious to him, since for our sake he reproves even kings. Where God is said to have come, apply this to the perception of the king, to whom the majesty of God was so manifested that he might clearly perceive himself divinely reproved and not deluded with a vain spectre. Then observe that although God reproved the king for Abraham’s sake, whom he covered with his special protection, he yet intends to show generally his displeasure against adultery: there is here no express mention of Abraham, but rather a general announcement made for the maintaining of conjugal fidelity — thou shalt die, because thou hast seized upon a woman who was joined to a husband. Let us learn that a precept was given in these words to mankind, forbidding any one to touch his neighbour’s wife; and since nothing in the life of man is more sacred than marriage, it is not to be wondered at that the Lord should require mutual fidelity. On the preservation, note that when the earlier account says she was taken by Pharaoh it does not say whether her chastity was assailed, but since the Lord then also declared himself the vindicator of her whom he now saved from dishonour, we ought not to doubt that her integrity was preserved both times — for why should he now forbid the king of Gerar to touch her, if he had previously suffered her to be corrupted in Egypt? See also that when the Lord so defers his aid as not to stretch out his hand till the faithful are in extreme peril, he shows the more clearly how admirable is his providence. As to the plea, call the explanation that Abimelech compares himself with the men of Sodom perhaps too refined, and prefer the simpler sense: O Lord, although thou dost severely punish adultery, shall thy wrath pour itself out on unoffending men, who have rather fallen into error than sinned knowingly and willingly? And mark in what way and to what extent he boasts his heart and hands guiltless: he does not arrogate to himself a purity altogether spotless, but only denies that he was led by lust, tyrannically or purposely, to abuse another man’s wife — and we know how great is the difference between an act of abandoned wickedness and a mere fault.

Observe that God revealed himself by dreams, which evidenced themselves to be divine and supernatural, not only to his servants the prophets but even to those outside the pale of the church and covenant; though usually it was with some regard to God’s own people, as in Pharaoh’s dream to Joseph, in Nebuchadnezzar’s to Daniel, and here in Abimelech’s to Abraham and Sarah, for he reproved this king for their sake. Note that God gives him notice of two dangers: the danger of sin, since the woman is a man’s wife and to take her is to wrong her husband; and the danger of death for that sin, for God’s saying of a man that he is a dead man makes him so. Every wilful sinner ought to be told that he is a dead man, as the condemned malefactor and the patient whose disease is mortal are said to be; if thou art a bad man, certainly thou art a dead man. Then observe how he pleads ignorance, that Abraham and Sarah had agreed to impose upon him and not to let him know they were any more than brother and sister; and see what confidence a man may have toward God when his heart condemns him not, for if our consciences witness to our integrity, and that however we may have been cheated into a snare we have not knowingly and wittingly sinned against God, it will be our rejoicing in the day of evil. Note too that he pleads with God as Abraham had done before him: wilt thou slay a righteous nation? — not such a nation as Sodom.

Observe that persons who were not of the family of Abraham had the knowledge of the true God, and indeed that all the Gerarites are termed a righteous nation. On the plea, say that had Abimelech had any other than honourable views in taking Sarah he could not have justified himself thus to his Maker, and that these views were of the most honourable kind God himself, to whom the appeal was made, asserts in the most direct manner when he says, Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart. Elsewhere say that God revealed himself by dreams, which evidenced themselves to be divine and supernatural, not only to his servants the prophets but even to those outside the pale of the church, though usually with some regard to God’s own people; and on the plea, that he asks whether God will slay a righteous nation, meaning not such a nation as Sodom.

debates: Whether the use of Elohim here marks a separate source from the parallel in Genesis 12.
Whether Abimelech was kept from Sarah by illness or by direct restraint.
Whether Abimelech is comparing his people to the men of Sodom.
How a polygamous king can be said to have acted in integrity of heart.
Whether the threat is aimed at Abraham’s case or lays down a general law.
outliers: Ellicott answers the documentary argument from the narrator’s own consistent rule about divine names.
Ellicott reads the threat medically, making the malady of the last verse the cause of the abstention.
Calvin calls the Sodom comparison too refined; Ellicott endorses it and names a scholar for it.
Ellicott concedes the king’s polygamy and harem rights and still allows the plea, on the principle of judgment according to knowledge.
Ellicott holds that nature does not give the moral law but only acknowledges it when revealed.
Calvin infers a general precept against adultery from the absence of Abraham’s name in the threat.
Calvin distinguishes a crime from a fault and confines Abimelech’s claim to the narrower denial.

6.pericope_label: And God said unto him in a dream, Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me — now therefore restore the man his wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live — therefore Abimelech rose early in the morning, and called all his servants, and told all these things in their ears: and the men were sore afraid

schools.summary: Infer from this answer of God that Abimelech did not testify falsely concerning his own integrity; yet while God allows the excuse to be true, he nevertheless chastises him. Learn hence that even they who are pure according to human judgment are not entirely free from blame, for no error may be deemed so excusable as to be without some deteriorating admixture; it is not for any one to absolve himself by his own judgment, but let us bring all our conduct to the standard of God, since it is not said in vain that the ways of men seem right to themselves but the Lord pondereth the hearts. And if even they who are unconscious to themselves of any evil do not escape censure, what will be our condition if we are held inwardly bound by our own conscience? Note that the declaration about withholding implies God had respect not only to Abraham but to the king, for because he had no intention of defiling another man’s wife God had compassion on him; and it frequently happens that the Spirit restrains with his bridle those who are gliding into error, just as, on the other hand, he drives headlong by infatuations and a spirit of stupor those who knowingly transgress with depraved affections. As God brought the heathen king a timely remedy that his guilt should not be increased, so he proves himself daily the faithful guardian of his own people, to prevent them from rushing from lighter faults into desperate crimes. On the title, say God does not now speak of Abraham as of a common man but as of one so peculiarly dear to himself that he undertakes the defence of his conjugal bed by a kind of privilege; he calls him a prophet for the sake of honour, as if charging Abimelech with having injured a man of singular excellence, that he might not wonder at the greatness of the punishment. And although the word prophet is properly the name of an office, take it here in a more comprehensive import, for a chosen man familiar with God: since at that time no Scripture was in existence, God not only made himself known by dreams and visions but chose to himself rare and excellent men to scatter abroad the seed of piety, by which the world would become the more inexcusable. But since Abraham is a prophet, he is constituted as it were a mediator between God and Abimelech. Christ even then was the only Mediator, but this was no reason why some men should not pray for others, especially they who excelled in holiness and were accepted by God, as the apostle teaches that the fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much; and we ought not at this day to neglect such intercession, provided it does not obscure the grace of Christ nor lead us away from him. But that under this pretext the Papists resort to the patronage of the dead is absurd: for as the Lord does not here send the king of Gerar to Noah or to any one of the dead fathers, but into the presence of the living Abraham, so neither may they. On the morning, show how efficacious the oracle had been: Abimelech, alarmed at the voice of God, arose not only that he might quickly obey the command enjoined upon him, but that he might also exhort his own people to do the same. An example of such ready obedience is shown us in a heathen king, that we may no more make excuses for our torpor when we are so little profited by the divine remonstrances — God appeared to him in a dream, but since he daily cries aloud in our ears by the law, by the prophets, by the apostles, and finally by his only-begotten Son, it were absurd to suppose that so many testimonies should avail less than the vision of a single dream. Elsewhere say the same dream continued; that restoring the wife will be a full proof to all of the integrity of heart and innocence of hands which he pleads and which God owns; and that Abimelech, awaking upon the dream, could sleep no more, his thoughts running on what had been said to him, so that as soon as it was light he rose from his bed.

Say that he is a prophet is not an aggravation of Abimelech’s sin but an encouragement to him to restore Sarah, and is therefore rightly joined with the words he shall pray for thee. Take the word prophet here in its old sense of spokesman, and especially of one who mediates between God and man. There was a true feeling that God in his own nature is beyond the reach of man, and this in heathen nations led to men peopling their heavens with a multitude of minor deities; in Israel, after the founding of the prophetic schools, the prophets became an order whose office was partly to enliven the services of the Temple with sacred minstrelsy but chiefly to be God’s spokesmen, declaring his will to Jew and Gentile and maintaining religion and holiness by earnest preaching. In this way they were forerunners, and even representatives, of Christ, who is the one true and only Mediator between God and man; and not only Abraham but the patriarchs generally are called Christs and prophets, as being speakers for God to man and for man to God, until the true Christ and prophet came. Add that Abimelech is thus taught that he does not himself hold a near relation to God but requires some one to speak for him; and that perhaps he would gather from it that he had need of fuller instruction, and ought to try to attain a higher level, Abraham becoming a prophet to him in the other sense of teacher.

Observe that Abimelech, being warned of God in a dream, takes the warning, and as one truly afraid of sin and its consequences rises early to obey the directions given him. Note his caution to his servants: Abraham himself could not be more careful to command his household in this matter, and those whom God has convinced of sin and danger ought to tell others what God has done for their souls, that they also may be awakened and brought to a like holy fear. Then note his chiding of Abraham, and the serious reproof he gave him: his reasoning on this occasion was very strong and yet very mild, and nothing could be said better, for he does not reproach him nor insult over him, does not say, Is this your profession? I see, though you will not swear, you will lie; if these be prophets, I will beg to be freed from the sight of them — but he fairly represents the injury Abraham had done him and calmly signifies his resentment of it. Observe that he calls the sin he had been in danger of a great sin, for even the light of nature teaches men that the sin of adultery is a very great sin, be it observed to the shame of many who call themselves Christians and yet make a light matter of it. Observe that he looks upon it that both himself and his kingdom would have been exposed to the wrath of God had he been guilty of this sin, though ignorantly, from which note that the sins of kings often prove the plagues of kingdoms, and that rulers should therefore, for their people’s sake, dread sin.

Say it is God that restrains men from doing the ill they would do; it is not from him that there is sin, but it is from him that there is not more sin, either by his influence on men’s minds checking their inclination to sin, or by his providence taking away the opportunity — and that it is a great mercy to be hindered from committing sin, which God must have the glory of, whoever is the instrument. On the title of prophet, argue that the word, which we have from the Greek and which is compounded of before and I speak, means in its general acceptation one who speaks of things before they happen; but that this was not the original notion of the word, as its use in this place sufficiently proves, since Abraham certainly was not a prophet in the present acceptation of the term. For the Hebrew word we must seek some other meaning, and the proper ideal meaning of the original is to pray, entreat, make supplication, which may be justified both from its application here and from its pointed use in the case of Saul, and from the case of the priests of Baal, where prophesying most undoubtedly means making prayer and supplication. As those who were in habits of intimacy with God by prayer and faith were found the most proper persons to communicate his mind to man, both with respect to the present and the future, hence the intercessor became in process of time the public instructor or preacher, and also the predictor of future events, because to such faithful praying men God revealed the secret of his will — whence the apostle seems to restrain the word wholly to the interpreting of the mind of God to the people and their instruction in divine things, for he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification and exhortation and comfort. Refer the reader to your own discourse on the subject. And on the morning, say that as the day broke he arose, assembled his servants, and communicated what he had received from God; that they were all struck with astonishment and discerned the hand of God in the business; and that Abraham was then called, and in a most respectful and pious manner the king expostulated with him for bringing him and his people under the divine displeasure by withholding the information that Sarah was his wife, when by taking her he sought only an honourable alliance with his family.

debates: What the word prophet means when it is first used in Scripture.
Whether the title is given Abraham as an office or as an honour.
Whether one man’s intercession for another warrants invoking the departed.
Whether a man acquitted of intent is thereby acquitted of blame.
How Abimelech knew to take the dream as divine.
outliers: Clarke argues from three passages that the Hebrew word for prophet properly means to pray or make supplication.
Ellicott takes prophet in the sense of spokesman and makes the whole order a forerunner of the one Mediator.
Calvin turns Abraham’s mediation against invoking the dead, since the king is sent to a living intercessor.
Calvin holds that no error is so excusable as to be without some deteriorating admixture, even when God allows the plea.
Wesley formulates the doctrine of restraint: sin is not from God, but it is from God that there is not more sin.
Henry admires the mildness of the heathen king’s reproof and writes the speech he might have made instead.
Calvin argues from the lesser to the greater, that one dream moved a heathen where law, prophets, apostles and the Son move us little.

9.pericope_label: Then Abimelech called Abraham, and said unto him, What hast thou done unto us? and what have I offended thee, that thou hast brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin? — and Abimelech said unto Abraham, What sawest thou, that thou hast done this thing? — and Abraham said, Because I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife’s sake

schools.summary: Note that some suppose the king of Gerar did not make a complaint against Abraham but rather declared his own repentance; yet if we fairly weigh his words we find confession mixed with expostulation. Although he complains that Abraham had acted unjustly, he does not so transfer the blame as to free himself from all fault, and he may with justice impute part of the blame to Abraham, provided he also acknowledges his own sin. Know therefore that this king did not act as hypocrites are in the habit of doing: for as soon as ever a pretext is furnished for inculpating others, they confidently absolve themselves, and even esteem it a lawful purgation if they can draw others into a participation of their crime. But Abimelech, while he complains that he had been deceived, does not scruple to condemn himself as guilty of a great sin. No one, then, may exonerate himself from blame under the pretence that he had been induced by others to sin. Note also that adultery is here called a great sin because it binds not one man only but a whole people, as in a common crime; the king could not have spoken thus had he not acknowledged the sacred right of marriage — whereas at the present time Christians, at least they who boast of the name, are not ashamed jocularly to extenuate so great a crime, from which even a heathen shrinks with the greatest horror. On the second question, observe that by it the king provides against the future: he thinks Abraham had not practised this dissimulation inconsiderately, and since God was grievously offended he fears to fall again into the same danger, so that by an inquiry so earnest he testifies that he wishes to remedy the evil. And note that it is no common sign of a just and meek disposition in Abimelech that he allows Abraham a free defence; we know how sharply and fiercely they expostulate who think themselves aggrieved, so much the greater praise was due to the moderation of this king toward an unknown foreigner — let us learn by his example, whenever we expostulate with brethren who may have wronged us, to permit them freely to answer. On the defence itself, note two points: first, he confesses that fear induced him to conceal his marriage; then he denies that he lied in order to excuse himself. Although he declares truly that he had not concealed the marriage with any fraudulent intention nor to injure any one, he was worthy of censure, because through fear he had submitted, so far as in him lay, to the prostitution of his wife. Much cannot be said in his excuse, since he ought to have been more courageous and resolute in fulfilling the duty of a husband, vindicating the honour of his wife whatever danger might threaten him; besides, it was a sign of distrust to resort to an unlawful subtlety. As to his suspicion, although he had everywhere perceived that a monstrous licentiousness prevailed, it was nevertheless unjust to form so unfavourable a judgment of a people he had not yet known, for he supposes them all to be homicides. We conclude that Abraham does not contend for the justice of his cause before God, but only shows his earnestness to appease Abimelech. His form of expression is, however, to be noticed: for wherever the fear of God does not reign, men easily rush onward to every kind of wickedness, so that they neither spare human blood nor restrain themselves from rapine and violence; and it is the fear of God alone which unites us in the bonds of our common humanity.

Give the verses, then the substance. Take the second question to mean, What hadst thou in thine eye with thine act, that is with thy false statement; though some modern commentators explain the Hebrew so, the old rendering is probably right, since Abimelech first denies by indignant questions that he had been guilty of any wrong toward Abraham, and then asks what he had seen in the conduct of himself and his people to justify such mistrust. Observe that throughout the king speaks as a man conscious that his citizens so respected the rights of a stranger and of marriage that Sarah would have been perfectly safe had Abraham openly said she was his wife. Note that Abimelech made his complaint publicly in the presence of his servants, partly for his own justification in the sight of his dependents and partly to put Abraham to shame; and that Abraham had but two weak excuses, first that he supposed there was no fear of God at all in the land and trembled for his life because of his wife, and second that when he left his father’s house he had arranged with his wife that in every foreign place she should call herself his sister, as she really was his half-sister. Notice too how, on the subject of his emigration, he expressed himself indefinitely and with reserve, accommodating himself to the polytheistic standpoint of the Philistine king. On the first excuse, say Abraham’s general condemnation of the people had some excuse in the widespread depravity of the nations in Canaan, but was nevertheless unjust: even those nations were not utterly corrupt, and both in Egypt and in Gerar the standard of morality was higher than he supposed, his difficulty being the result of his own imperfect faith. But add the other side: the fact that this artifice was arranged between man and wife when starting on their long wanderings proves that they rather over-rated than under-rated the risks that lay before them. The expedient was indeed a sorry one, and shows that Abraham’s faith was not yet that of a martyr; but it also shows that both of them felt that he might have to save his life by a means almost as bad as death — and thus, after all, it was no commonplace faith, but one as firm at root as it was sorely tried and exercised.

See here much to blame, even in the father of the faithful. Mark his distrust of God, his undue care about life, his intent to deceive. He also threw temptation in the way of others, caused affliction to them, exposed himself and Sarah to just rebukes, and yet attempted an excuse. These things are written for our warning, not for us to imitate. Even Abraham hath not whereof to glory: he cannot be justified by his works, but must be indebted for justification to that righteousness which is upon all and unto all them that believe. We must not condemn all as hypocrites who fall into sin, if they do not continue in it; but let the unhumbled and impenitent take heed that they do not sin on, thinking that grace may abound.

Say that equivocation and dissimulation, however they may be palliated, are very ill things, and by no means to be admitted in any case; that the king takes it as a very great injury to himself and his family that Abraham had thus exposed them to sin; and that his complaint amounts to this, that if I had been thy worst enemy thou couldst not have done me a worse turn, nor taken a more effectual course to be avenged on me. Note that we ought to reckon that those do us the greatest unkindness in the world who any way tempt us or expose us to sin, though they may pretend friendship and offer that which is grateful enough to corrupt nature; and that he challenges Abraham to assign any just cause he had to suspect them as a dangerous people for an honest man to live among. On the answer, say it is the best excuse he could make for his conduct, which in this instance is far from defensible; and then draw the warning: there are many places and persons that have more of the fear of God in them than we think they have — perhaps they are not called by our name, they do not wear our badges, they do not tie themselves to that which we have an opinion of, and therefore we conclude they have not the fear of God in their hearts.

debates: Whether Abimelech is accusing Abraham or confessing his own fault.
Whether Abraham’s suspicion of the men of Gerar was just.
What the second question means, what didst thou see or what didst thou intend.
Whether the standing arrangement tells for or against Abraham’s faith.
Why adultery is called a great sin here.
outliers: Calvin refuses to let a genuine grievance excuse the man who holds it, and makes Abimelech the model of the distinction.
Ellicott turns the pre-arranged deception into evidence that the couple over-rated the danger, and so into evidence of real faith.
Keil and Delitzsch note that Abraham accommodates his language to the polytheism of the king he is answering.
Wesley warns that men outside our name and badges may have more of the fear of God than we suppose.
Calvin praises a heathen king for allowing the accused a free defence, and makes it a rule for Christians.
Calvin rebukes his own contemporaries for jesting at a sin from which a heathen shrank with horror.
Ellicott reads the king’s questions as the words of a man confident of his own people’s morals.

12.pericope_label: And yet indeed she is my sister; she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife — and it came to pass, when God caused me to wander from my father’s house, that I said unto her, This is thy kindness which thou shalt shew unto me; at every place whither we shall come, say of me, He is my brother — and Abimelech took sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants, and gave them unto Abraham, and restored him Sarah his wife

schools.summary: On the relationship, note that some suppose Sarah to have been Abraham’s own sister, not by the same mother but born of a second wife; but since the name sister has a wider signification among the Hebrews, adopt rather the conjecture that she was his sister in the second degree, so that they had a common father, that is a grandfather, from whom they had descended by brothers. Observe that Abraham extenuates his offence and draws a distinction between his silence and a direct falsehood, and that he professed with truth that he was the brother of Sarah, feigning nothing in words which differed from the facts. Yet when all things have been sifted, his defence proves either frivolous or too feeble: since he had purposely used the name of sister as a pretext, lest men should have any suspicion of his marriage, he sophistically afforded them an occasion of falling into error, so that although he did not lie in words, with respect to the matter of fact his dissimulation was a lie by implication. He had, however, no other intention than to declare that he had not dealt fraudulently with Abimelech, but that in an affair of great anxiety he had caught at an indirect method of escape from death. On the plural verb, since it is here put in the plural number, expound the passage freely as referring to the angels who led Abraham through his various wanderings; and say that some with too much subtlety infer from it a Trinity of Persons. Grant that the plural noun is frequently taken for God in Scripture, but insist that then the verb with which it is connected is always singular, and that wherever a plural verb is added it signifies angels or princes. Then reject the accommodation reading: there are those who think that Abraham, because he was speaking with one not rightly instructed, spoke thus in conformity with the common custom of the heathen; but this is most erroneous, for to what purpose did he, by erecting altars, make it manifest that he was devoted to the service of the only true God, if it were lawful for him afterwards to deny in words the very God whom he had worshipped? On the presents, note that Abraham had before received gifts in Egypt, but with this difference, that whereas the one king commanded him to depart elsewhere, this one offers him a home in his kingdom. Both kings were stricken with no common degree of fear, for when they perceived that they were reproved by the Lord for having troubled Abraham, they found no method of appeasing God except by compensating with acts of kindness for the injury they had brought on the holy man. The difference flowed hence, that the first, being more severely censured, was so terrified that he could scarcely bear the sight of Abraham, whereas this one, although alarmed, was soon composed by an added word of consolation, when the Lord said, He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee — for there is no other remedy for the removal of fear than the Lord’s declaration that he will be propitious. It is of little advantage for the sinner to present to God only what fear extorts; but it is a true sign of penitence when, with a composed mind and quiet conscience, he yields himself obedient and docile to God. And since Abimelech allowed Abraham a habitation in his realm, a blessing of no trivial kind followed this act of humanity, because Isaac was born there. Elsewhere note that she was sister to Lot, both being children of Haran the brother of Abraham; that the word for God is here in the plural, with the verb agreeing, and that this is not to be taken of the idol gods of the Gentiles as one Targum interprets it, but of the true God, as the Jewish commentators acknowledge and as many Christian interpreters understand of the three Persons in the Godhead; and that the gifts were given that Abraham might pray and intercede for the king and his family, since he had learned from the divine oracle that he was a prophet.

Say that the clause about the mother disproves the notion that Sarah was the same as Iscah; for as Iscah was Terah’s granddaughter, the distinction between the identity of the father and the diversity of the mother would in her case be unmeaning. Sarah was apparently Abraham’s half-sister, Terah’s daughter by another wife; and we gather from her name, that is princely, that she was not a concubine but belonged to some noble race. On the verb, state the rule: according to rule the plural noun for God is construed with a verb singular for the true God, but with a verb plural for false gods. Here the verb is plural, and the same construction occurs in four other places, while in a fifth the noun is joined with an adjective in the plural. These exceptions may either be relics of a less strict use of the name, or they may be errors of copyists misled by the ordinary rules of grammar — and this latter view is confirmed by the fact that the Samaritan Pentateuch, both here and in one of the parallels, has the singular. On the compact, note that the fact of its having been made so long before would convince Abimelech that their conduct was not occasioned by anything they had seen at Gerar. And on the presents, contrast the two kings: the earlier gave his when he took Sarah, and though he did not exact them back he bade Abraham go his way in displeasure; more generously, the Philistine gives presents on restoring Sarah, grants her husband permission to dwell in his land wherever it pleased him, and thereby acknowledges that he had done Abraham a wrong.

Set out the kindness of a prince which Abimelech showed to Abraham, and see how unjust Abraham’s jealousies were: he fancied that if they knew Sarah was his wife they would kill him, but when they did know it, instead of killing him they were kind to him, frightened at least to be so by the divine rebukes they were under. He gives him his royal licence to dwell where he pleased in his country, courting his stay; and he gives him royal gifts, sheep and oxen and a thousand pieces of silver, when he restores Sarah — either by way of satisfaction for the wrong he had offered in taking her to his house, as when the Philistines restored the ark, being plagued for detaining it, they sent a present with it, and as the law appointed that when restitution was made something should be added to it; or to engage Abraham’s prayers for him, not as if prayers should be bought and sold, but because we should endeavour to be kind to those of whose spiritual things we reap. Note that it is our wisdom to get and keep an interest with those that have an interest in heaven, and to make those our friends who are the friends of God. And note that he gives Sarah good instruction, calling her husband her brother to upbraid her with having called him so, and telling her that he must be to her for a covering of the eyes, that is, she must look at no other nor desire to be looked at by any other — for yoke-fellows must be to each other a covering of the eyes.

Answer the half-truth plainly: I have not told a lie, I have suppressed only a part of the truth — and then ask what a lie is. It is any action done or word spoken, whether true or false in itself, which the doer or speaker wishes the observer or hearer to take in a contrary sense to that which he knows to be true; it is, in a word, any action done or speech delivered with the intention to deceive, though both may be absolutely true and right in themselves. On the parentage, preserve the ancient tradition that Terah first married one wife, by whom he had Abraham, and afterwards another, by whom he had Sarah, so that she was his sister by the same father and a different mother. On the plural verb, note that the word for God is here used with a plural verb, which is not very usual in Hebrew, since this plural noun is generally joined with verbs in the singular; and because there is a departure from the general mode in this instance, some have contended that the word signifies princes here, and suppose it to refer to those in Chaldea who expelled Abraham because he would not worship the fire — but the best critics, and with them the Jews, allow that it signifies the true God, and Abraham probably refers to his first call. And on the compact, say that then they settled this matter; that it may be God denied Abraham and Sarah the blessing of children so long to punish them for this sinful compact they had made to deny one another, for if they will not own their marriage, why should God own it? But suppose that after this reproof they agreed never to do so again, and note that presently we read that Sarah conceived.

debates: What relation Sarah actually bore to Abraham.
Whether a true statement made to deceive is a lie.
Why the word for God takes a plural verb in this verse.
Whether Abraham accommodated his language to a heathen hearer.
Why the two kings treated Abraham so differently.
outliers: Clarke defines a lie by intent rather than content, so that a true statement may be one.
Calvin agrees, holding that Abraham did not lie in words but that his dissimulation was a lie by implication.
Ellicott states the rule for the divine name, lists the exceptions, and prefers to treat them as copyists’ errors.
Calvin reads the plural of angels and dismisses the Trinitarian inference as too subtle.
Calvin calls the accommodation reading most erroneous, though Keil and Delitzsch adopt it earlier in this same chapter.
The editorial matter printed with Calvin argues against him in his own margin.
Wesley suggests that Sarah’s long barrenness was a punishment for the compact to deny the marriage.

15.pericope_label: And Abimelech said, Behold, my land is before thee: dwell where it pleaseth thee — and unto Sarah he said, Behold, I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver: behold, he is to thee a covering of the eyes, unto all that are with thee, and with all other: thus she was reproved — so Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children — for the Lord had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham’s wife

schools.summary: Note that instead of bidding him be gone and sending him away in haste, as the king of Egypt did in a like case, this king solicits his stay and makes an offer of his whole kingdom, to choose what part of it he would dwell in. On the money, reckon a thousand shekels at about a hundred and twenty-five pounds of our money, though perhaps little pieces of silver current in that country are meant which were not worth so much; and note that some think the sheep and oxen were worth so many pieces, though it rather seems he gave these over and above, and chiefly for Sarah’s use, since the words are directed to her — and in them there is a sharp cutting expression, calling Abraham her brother and not her husband, thereby upbraiding her with her equivocation and dissimulation. Because there is some obscurity in the words, note that the passage is variously explained, though the beginning of the verse is free from difficulty: when the king had given a thousand pieces of silver, then in order that his liberality might not be suspected he declares that he had given them to Abraham, and that since Abraham had been honourably received his wife was not to be regarded as a harlot. But what follows is more obscure. Many interpreters refer the covering to the gift, in which they seem to be wrong: the Hebrews, having no neuter gender, use the feminine instead, but here the husband is rather pointed to, and this best suits the sense — for Sarah is taught that the husband to whom she is joined was as a veil with which she ought to be covered, lest she should be exposed to others. The apostle says that the veil which the woman carries on her head is the symbol of subjection; this belongs also to unmarried persons, as referring to the end for which the sex is ordained, but it applies more aptly to married women, because they are veiled as by the very ordinance of marriage. Explain the words therefore thus: thou, if thou hadst no husband, wouldst be exposed to many dangers, but now, since God has appointed for thee a guardian of thy modesty, it behoves thee to conceal thyself under that veil — why then hast thou of thine own accord thrown off this covering? This was a just censure, because Sarah, by pretending, had deprived herself of the divine protection. On the healing, note that in two respects the wonderful favour of God toward Abraham was apparent: that with outstretched hand he avenged the injury done him, and that through Abraham’s prayer he became pacified toward the house of Abimelech — and it was necessary to declare that the house had been healed in answer to those prayers, that the inhabitants might be the more closely bound to him. But raise the difficulty of the punishment described in the whole house being barren: for if Abraham had gone into the land of Gerar after Sarah had conceived, and if all that is here related was fulfilled before Isaac was born, how was it possible that in so short a time this sterility should be manifest? If we should say that the judgment of God was then made plain in a manner unknown to us, the answer would not be inappropriate; yet it is not certain that the series of the history has not been inverted, and the more probable supposition may seem to be that Abraham had already been resident in Gerar when Isaac was promised to him, the part before omitted being now inserted. Since the correct notation of time does little to confirm our faith, leave both opinions undecided. Elsewhere say the wombs were closed with large tumours, so that they could neither cohabit nor bring forth, and that this was inflicted to rebuke and punish the taking of Sarah into the house.

Give the verses, and then the substance: after this reparation, God healed Abimelech at Abraham’s intercession, and also his wife and maids, so that they could bear again, for the Lord had closed up every womb in the house on Sarah’s account. Distinguish the words carefully: the maids here are those whom the king kept as concubines, and are to be distinguished from the female slaves named earlier, a material difference proved by a passage in Samuel; and the phrase for closing every womb does not mean, as is frequently supposed, to prevent actual childbirth, but to prevent conception, that is to produce barrenness, as is evident from the expression He hath restrained me from bearing. On the money, take a thousand of silver as the total value of the present and not an additional gift, about a hundred and twenty-five pounds, a large sum at a time when silver was scarce and dear. Then take the difficult speech apart. It begins with a touch of irony in calling Abraham thy brother. Next, if the pronoun is translated in the masculine, the meaning would be that Abraham ought to have been Sarah’s protector but had failed in this duty; more probably it is neuter and refers to the gift. The covering of the eyes may mean a veil to protect her from the wanton desires of others, or to conceal her shame at the wrong done her. Finally the verb rendered reproved is equivocal and should rather be translated righted; it may be third person feminine as in our version, or second person, in which case it is part of the king’s speech, and the clause and with all must then be taken with the verb. Render the whole probably thus: Behold, I have given thy brother a gift worth a thousand pieces of silver: behold, it shall be to thee for a covering of the eyes to all that are with thee — that is, so large a compensation for the wrong done thee in taking thee from thy husband will be a proof to all thy friends and attendants that thou hast not been disgraced but treated with honour — and in respect of all that has happened thou art thus righted. On the prayer, say that as Abimelech had now made very liberal compensation it became Abraham’s duty to intercede for him, and that the malady seems to have been confined to the king, its object being to protect Sarah, though in some way it so affected the whole household as to produce general barrenness.

Admit at once that here there is scarcely any agreement among interpreters, that the Hebrew is exceedingly obscure, and that every interpreter takes it in his own sense. Take the thousand pieces to be shekels, note that the Greek version renders them didrachms, and that since the verb signifies literally to weigh and the shekel was a coin of such a weight, some think this the origin of our word scale, the instrument to weigh with; report that the shekel of the sanctuary weighed twenty gerahs, that according to the Jews the gerah weighed sixteen grains of barley, and that one rabbi observes the shekel was increased after the captivity — while confessing that on the subject of ancient weights and measures very little that is satisfactory is known. Then take the covering as neuter: it, the thousand shekels, and not he, Abraham, is to thee for a covering, to procure thee a veil to conceal thy beauty from all thy own kindred and acquaintance and from all strangers, that none, seeing thou art another man’s wife, may covet thee on account of thy comeliness. Take the closing verb as a second person preterite used for the imperative, from a root meaning to make straight or to speak rightly. Or else say only that thy brother is to thee a covering of the eyes: thou must look at no other, nor desire to be looked at by any other, for yoke-fellows must be to each other a covering of the eyes, the marriage covenant being a covenant with the eyes. On the prayer, note that this was the prime office of the prophet as the word was earlier explained. And on the barrenness, say it was probably by means of some disease with which they had been smitten, since they are said to be healed at Abraham’s intercession, and that possibly this same disease had afflicted the king and was the means by which he was withheld. Then end with the warning: the cause why the patriarch did not acknowledge his wife was a fear that he should lose his life on her account, for he said, Surely the fear of the true God is not in this place. Such is the natural bigotry and narrowness of the human heart that we can scarcely allow that any besides ourselves possess the true religion, and to indulge such a disposition is highly blamable. The true religion is neither confined to one spot nor to one people; it is spread in various forms over the whole earth, and he who fills immensity has left a record of himself in every nation and among every people under heaven. Beware of the spirit of intolerance, for bigotry produces uncharitableness, and uncharitableness harsh judging, and in such a spirit a man may think he does God service when he tortures the person whom his narrow mind and hard heart have dishonoured with the name of heretic.

debates: Whether the covering of the eyes is the gift or the husband.
Whether the closing verb reproves Sarah or vindicates her.
Whether the barrenness prevented conception or birth.
Whether the events of this chapter stand in their chronological place.
What a thousand pieces of silver amounted to.
outliers: Clarke opens by conceding that the Hebrew is obscure and every interpreter takes it in his own sense.
Calvin names and rejects the reading Clarke adopts, making the husband and not the money the veil.
Ellicott renders the verb righted rather than reproved, turning a rebuke of Sarah into a public vindication of her.
Calvin cannot reconcile the barrenness with the chronology and suspects the history has been inverted.
Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the king’s concubines from his slave women on the strength of a passage in Samuel.
Clarke turns Abraham’s misjudgment of Gerar into a warning that bigotry ends in burning heretics.
Gill and Ellicott independently value the gift at about a hundred and twenty-five pounds.
